body_en:
A Chinese delivery rider in Australia was stabbed to death by a homeless man. The whole city fell silent for him; all of Australia stood in solemn mourning. Local public figures came on their own to pay their respects and speak for him, and promised that compensation would reach his family soon.

A Chinese man living far from home, mourned by an entire city and remembered by everyone. Local figures vowed to get justice for him.

A nobody who only ever knew how to work and give — on the day he died, a city remembered him.

Every person can be remembered by the world, no matter their rank or trade, their height or weight.

At Arlington National Cemetery, every citizen who died for the country is honored, every name equal regardless of rank. The Chinese laborers long forgotten back home are remembered by the world — at the Chinese Labour Corps memorial in Britain, the names of every laborer who worked there are written out in dense rows, and every year they are honored as heroes. Every one of them, by name, is treated as a hero.

And Australia is no less. Its grandest stage now honors an extraordinary ordinary man. He was ordinary, unremarkable, even lowly — so lowly that he fought with everything he had to protect a single delivery, because losing it would have meant a 50-Australian-dollar fine from the platform, and he kept fighting until a thug stabbed him to death. Maybe, like countless other nobodies, he would simply have died cold and alone; maybe, like one data point after another, he would have gone quiet and vanished.

Perhaps millions like him have long been ignored by the world. But he will not be forgotten. He was only an ordinary Chinese man — and at the same time, he stood for millions of fathers and families. The world prospers because of countless people like him. He is a hero, a Chinese hero worth remembering by everyone — a hero who fought to survive, a Chinese man who fought to protect his family.

Thank you, warm city, for standing up for this Chinese man. For giving him justice. For letting us believe that the fate handed down since the first emperor — of people being treated as expendable statistics — has finally been broken, here and now. From this moment on, every person will have a name of their own, and like everyone in the world who loves life and lives for the world, will leave behind an extraordinary name.
excerpt_en: A Chinese food delivery rider in Australia was stabbed to death by a homeless man, and the whole city fell silent in mourning. Local figures came to pay their respects and promised his family would be looked after.
title_en: The Death of a Chinese Delivery Rider That Brought a Whole City to Silence
